en: Extremely miserable or hopeless; completely without pride or dignity
hook: AB-JECT: thrown (ject) away (ab), cast down to the lowest point.
story: After the factory closed, the workers lived in abject poverty: no food, no savings, no hope. Their former boss, caught for fraud, offered an abject apology, groveling on live TV. Abject means extremely wretched, or humiliatingly without pride. An abject failure is total failure.

en: Friendly and without serious disagreement
hook: AMICABLE: AMIGO (friend) + able.
story: Although they decided to end their business partnership, the two friends kept it amicable: they divided everything fairly, shook hands, and still meet for tea every Friday. Amicable means friendly and peaceful. An amicable settlement avoids court battles.

en: Strong hostility or hatred
hook: ANIMOSITY: like ANIMALS growling at each other.
story: The animosity between the two rival football clubs was so intense that their fans couldn't sit in the same section of the stadium. Animosity is strong, active hostility. Synonyms: animus, enmity, rancor.

en: To state or assert something to be true, firmly
hook: AVER: 'A-VERity', declaring the truth.
story: Despite all the evidence against him, the accused man continued to aver his innocence: 'I was at my sister's house that night. I swear it.' To aver is to assert firmly. Synonyms: affirm, declare, maintain.

en: An overwhelming outpouring of many things at once
hook: BARRAGE: like a BARRAGE of artillery fire.
story: After the press conference, the minister faced a barrage of questions from fifty reporters, all shouting at once. A barrage is a rapid, overwhelming flood of something: questions, criticism, or bullets. Synonyms: onslaught, deluge.

en: Providing emotional release and relief
hook: CATHARTIC: a CAT-HEART cleanse — releases what's trapped inside.
story: After months of stress, Mitu cried for an hour while watching a sad movie. Afterwards, she felt lighter, as if a weight had lifted. It was cathartic. Cathartic means providing emotional release. Writing in a journal can be cathartic.

en: To figure out the meaning of something hard to read or understand
hook: DE-CIPHER: undo the CIPHER (code).
story: The pharmacist squinted at the doctor's handwriting, trying to decipher whether it said 'twice daily' or 'twice weekly.' To decipher is to decode or interpret something difficult. Scholars spent years deciphering ancient scripts.

en: A false belief held firmly despite evidence against it
hook: DELUSION: an ILLUSION you won't let go of.
story: Tanvir was under the delusion that he could prepare for the GRE in one week; even after failing three practice tests, he still believed it. A delusion is a firmly held false belief. Delusions of grandeur mean believing you're far more important than you are.

en: To distribute; to provide (a service)
hook: DISPENSE: like a water DISPENSER giving out water.
story: The village doctor dispensed free medicine every Friday, and on Saturdays he dispensed advice to anyone who asked. To dispense is to give out. To dispense with something means to get rid of it: let's dispense with formalities.

en: Fluent, persuasive, and expressive in speaking or writing
hook: E-LOQU-ENT: 'loqu' means speak. Speaks beautifully.
story: The student's eloquent speech at graduation moved the whole hall to tears; every word was clear, powerful, and perfectly chosen. Eloquent means fluent and persuasive. Sometimes silence can be eloquent too, expressing more than words.

en: To capture someone's complete attention; to fascinate
hook: ENTHRALL: like a THRALL (slave) to the story.
story: The magician enthralled the children; for an hour, not a single one looked away or made a sound. To enthrall is to captivate completely. A good novel can enthrall you until three in the morning.

en: To destroy or get rid of completely
hook: E-RADIC-ATE: pull out by the ROOTS (radix).
story: Thanks to a worldwide vaccination campaign, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980. The last natural case of its deadliest form was a little girl on Bhola Island, Bangladesh, in 1975. To eradicate is to destroy completely, pulling something out by the roots. Bangladesh aims to eradicate extreme poverty.

en: New and inexperienced; a young bird just learning to fly
hook: FLEDGLING: a baby bird just getting its feathers.
story: Arif's fledgling startup had three employees, one office chair, and big dreams. Like a young bird learning to fly, it wobbled, but it kept going. Fledgling means new and inexperienced. A fledgling democracy is young and still fragile.

en: Courage and strength of mind in facing pain or adversity
hook: FORTITUDE: a FORT inside your mind.
story: After losing her home in the river erosion, the widow rebuilt her life with remarkable fortitude: no complaints, just steady work, one day at a time. Fortitude means courage in the face of adversity. It takes fortitude to keep studying after repeated failures.

en: Happening by chance, especially lucky chance
hook: FORTUITOUS: FORTUNE-ate by chance.
story: Sara's meeting with the professor was fortuitous; they happened to sit next to each other on a train, and he later became her research supervisor. Fortuitous means happening by chance, usually luckily. Synonym: serendipitous.

en: To provoke or urge someone into action
hook: GOAD: a pointed stick used to push cattle forward.
story: His friends goaded Rafi into jumping into the cold river: 'Coward! Do it!' He finally jumped and regretted it immediately. To goad is to provoke or push someone into action, like a farmer using a pointed stick on an ox.

en: About to happen
hook: IMMINENT: IN a MINute it will happen.
story: Black clouds, howling wind, and the radio warning: the cyclone's landfall was imminent. Families rushed to shelters. Imminent means about to happen very soon. Don't confuse it with eminent, which means famous.

en: Impossible to deny or dispute
hook: IN-CONTROVERT-IBLE: NO CONTROVERSY possible.
story: The DNA test provided incontrovertible proof; no lawyer could argue against it. The suspect finally confessed. Incontrovertible means impossible to deny. Synonyms: indisputable, irrefutable, undeniable.

en: Traveling from place to place
hook: ITINERANT: always following an ITINERARY.
story: The itinerant bioscope man traveled from village to village with his box of pictures, staying a few days in each place before moving on. Itinerant means traveling from place to place, especially for work. Itinerant workers follow the harvest.

en: Generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or weaker person
hook: MAGNA-NIMOUS: a MAGNIFICENT spirit (animus).
story: After winning the election, the new mayor was magnanimous: she invited her defeated rival to join her team and praised his ideas publicly. Magnanimous means generously forgiving, especially toward someone less powerful. A magnanimous winner shows grace.

en: Deserving praise or reward
hook: MERITORIOUS: full of MERIT.
story: The firefighter received a medal for meritorious service after rescuing twelve people from a burning building. Meritorious means deserving praise or reward. Synonyms: laudable, commendable, praiseworthy.

en: An open rebellion against authority, especially by soldiers or sailors
hook: MUTINY: the crew MUTES the captain and takes over.
story: Fed up with brutal treatment and rotten food, the ship's crew staged a mutiny, locking the captain in his cabin and sailing to the nearest port. A mutiny is open rebellion, especially by soldiers or sailors. Today, an office can face a mutiny too.

en: Seemingly contradictory but possibly true
hook: PARADOX: two contradictory things that are both true.
story: It sounds paradoxical, but the more Nadia rested, the faster she learned; short breaks helped her memory. Paradoxical means seemingly contradictory but true. 'Less is more' is a paradox. GRE passages love paradoxes.

en: Continued effort despite difficulty or delay
hook: PER-SEVERE-ANCE: persisting through SEVERE difficulty.
story: The rickshaw puller's son failed the university entrance exam twice. With perseverance, studying every night under a streetlight, he passed on his third try and later became an engineer. Perseverance means persistence despite difficulties.

en: To cause to become; to provide or give
hook: RENDER: RENDERS it into a new state.
story: The heavy flood rendered the bridge useless; no vehicle could cross. Volunteers rendered help to the stranded families. To render is to cause to become, or to provide. An artist renders a scene in paint; a computer renders 3D graphics.

en: The complete set of skills, songs, or works someone can perform
hook: REPERTOIRE: the REPORT of everything you can perform.
story: The singer's repertoire included two hundred songs: Rabindra Sangeet, folk songs, and modern pop. She could perform for six hours without repeating one. A repertoire is the collection of things you can do or perform. A good debater has a wide repertoire of arguments.

en: Able to recover quickly from difficulties
hook: RESILIENT: RE-SPRINGS back like a spring.
story: Bangladeshis are famously resilient: after every flood or cyclone, communities rebuild homes, replant crops, and reopen schools within weeks. Resilient means able to bounce back. A resilient material returns to its shape after being bent.

en: Firmly determined; unwavering
hook: RESOLUTE: full of RESOLVE.
story: Despite her family's objections, Mitu was resolute: she would become a pilot. She saved money, studied hard, and never wavered. Five years later, she flew her first plane. Resolute means firmly determined. Its opposite is irresolute.

en: Bending and moving easily; flexible
hook: SUPPLE: as soft and flexible as SUPPLE leather.
story: Years of yoga kept Grandma supple; at seventy, she could still touch her toes. The leather bag was supple and soft. Supple means flexible and bending easily. A supple mind adapts quickly to new ideas.

en: Great courage in the face of danger, especially in battle
hook: VALOR: VALUE of a hero's courage.
story: The freedom fighters of 1971 showed extraordinary valor, facing a powerful army with few weapons. Many were awarded the title Bir Sreshtho for their bravery. Valor means great courage, especially in battle. Valiant is the adjective.
